subject: Connectivity options for Maverick private deployment — VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Sanjay Rao <sanjay.rao@maverick.ai>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Cc: Lisa Cheng <lisa.cheng@maverick.ai>

Subject: Private deployment connectivity — quick guidance request

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the demo last week — the team is excited to move forward with Redwood Private. Before we schedule a full architecture review, we need a concise recommendation on connectivity patterns so we can line up network and procurement. Our environment: multi-account AWS (us-west-2 primary), on-prem MPLS with F5, strict egress controls, and SOC 2 + healthcare data scopes.

Specifically we want to understand:
- Tradeoffs (security/attack surface, latency, observability) between VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) and site-to-site VPN.
- Practical cards: which is easiest for a PoC vs production? Any blockers for cross-account setup?
- Estimated operational overhead and obvious gotchas (transitive routing, NAT, IP visibility).

We have an existing MPLS lat report attached (maverick_mpls_latency_report.pdf) and a high-level network diagram. Can you send a short write-up we can share with our NetOps and Security? If useful, Lisa and I are available for a 30-min call next week.

Thanks,

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
To: Sanjay Rao <sanjay.rao@maverick.ai>
Cc: Lisa Cheng <lisa.cheng@maverick.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity — quick guidance request

Sanjay / Lisa — thanks for the clear ask and the latency report. High level guidance below; I attached a matrix (connectivity_matrix_maverick_v1.xlsx) that maps each pattern to the requirements you listed.

TL;DR recommendation:
- PoC: start with a Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) from your on-prem/MPLS to a Redwood Private VPN endpoint. Fastest to stand up, good for validating traffic patterns and latency.
- Production (compliance + least surface area): prefer PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to expose only the Redwood inference endpoint(s) into your VPC(s) or account. PrivateLink gives stronger isolation and is easier to reason about for SOC 2 reviewers.
- VPC Peering: acceptable when both sides are in the same cloud account or trusted accounts in the same org and you need L3 flat connectivity. Not recommended if you require cross-account transitive routing or want to minimize East-West exposure.

Detailed tradeoffs — bullets so NetOps can skim:
- Security / attack surface:
  - PrivateLink: smallest service surface (single endpoint per region/account), supports endpoint policies. No public IPs.
  - VPC Peering: full-routed IPs between VPCs; increases blast radius. No privateDNS control beyond route tables.
  - S2S VPN: encrypted over WAN; surface area depends on on-prem firewall rules and NAT. Good short term but requires robust monitoring for drift.
- Latency / performance:
  - VPC Peering: lowest intra-region latency; not suitable across cloud regions without transit/peering mesh.
  - PrivateLink: slightly higher (~1–2 ms) than peering due to proxying but stable. Scales well for steady production traffic.
  - VPN: variable latency; depends on internet/MPLS path and device; not ideal for latency-sensitive inference at scale.
- Observability & IP visibility:
  - PrivateLink: Redwood presents service endpoints; you get target IPs in your subnet and can control logging at the endpoint.
  - Peering: full IP visibility; easier for teams that require source IP preservation, but more bookkeeping for route tables.
  - VPN: often NATted; source IPs may be translated unless you use route-based VPN with policy allowing original IPs.
- Ops / provisioning & cost:
  - PrivateLink: per-endpoint hourly cost + data processing; more predictable for production, simpler security reviews.
  - Peering: no per-GB charge but requires network engineering time for route table management and is non-transitive.
  - VPN: lowest upfront cost; higher ops overhead and potential egress/ingress charges depending on path.

Compliance and audits:
- For SOC 2 / HIPAA workloads we recommend PrivateLink for production because auditors prefer the constrained surface and explicit endpoint policies.
- We can provide network runbook artifacts and the SOC 2 evidence you asked for (see related links).

Suggested plan (fast, low risk):
1) Day 0–7: PoC with S2S VPN to validate traffic, authentication, and basic latency.
2) Day 7–21: Provision PrivateLink endpoints in target VPCs and validate failover and TLS.
3) Day 21+: Decommission the VPN or keep as backup/failover depending on SLA.

Action items:
- I attached the connectivity matrix and a short playbook (redwood_privatelink_playbook.docx).
- Ben — can you confirm Dedicated / Private capacity provisioning options and any endpoint service quotas we should flag?

Happy to join a call. Proposed slots: Tue 7/7 10:00–11:00 or Thu 7/9 09:00–10:00 PT.

Best,
Kimberly Park
Director, Solutions Architecture | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity — quick guidance request

Adding a few operational notes from the Dedicated/Private ops side:  

- PrivateLink endpoint service: we can publish an endpoint service in your account or in an account we manage. For cross-account setups we usually create a service and accept connection requests from your account to keep ownership clear (helps with billing and SLA mapping).
- VPC Peering caveat: AWS peering is not transitive. If you plan multiple customer VPCs + on-prem paths you will either need a transit gateway or manage peering pairs — both add complexity.
- NAT & source IPs: if preserving source IP is required for auditing, avoid SNAT on the VPN path; for PrivateLink we can forward original source IPs when endpoints are in your subnets, otherwise we recommend application-level headers to carry identity.
- Throughput: VPN appliances can rate-limit bursts; for production inference we size the gateway and recommend a validation run that simulates steady-state token throughput. Ben will coordinate a quick perf test if you want.

Kimberly — we can draft the MAP (mutual action plan) and include the SOC 2 networking artifacts. Sanjay / Lisa — I’ll take point on the capacity / endpoint request and confirm quota timelines (usually 5–7 business days for endpoint approvals with our infra).

—Ben
Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
